input.text: If you are a European rabbit, you can see all the way around you when you crouch in the freeze position, with a strip only 24 degrees wide in front where both eyes see the same thing. You have two kinds of color-sensing cell, blue and green, and you see about a tenth of the fine detail a human sees. Nobody has measured any of this in most other rabbits, hares and pikas, so for them it is unknown.
input.note: Left out pupil shape (R2) and tapetum (R7, R8) for length; R9 not used because it is a general statement for Leporidae.

input.text: Straight ahead of you is a wedge that both eyes see at once. If you are a red-tailed hawk or an American kestrel, that wedge is about 35 degrees wide, and if you are a bald eagle, it is about 40. For most hawks, eagles and falcons nobody has measured how much of the full circle your two eyes take in together.
input.note: Left out total field widths (R2 278, R30 300): their quotes give blind areas, not those values.

input.text: Nobody has measured how much ultraviolet, the light humans cannot see at all, reaches the eyes of a heron, egret, coot or dove, or how well they sense it. The shortest-wavelength color-sensing cell has been measured in the rock pigeon and the wild turkey, and in both it peaks in violet, at about 410 and 420 nanometers. In the whooping crane it peaks at about 405, so if you are a sandhill crane you very likely have a similar cell.
input.note: Left out the peafowl and quail figures, since they belong to those species. No record gives an ultraviolet range for any heron, crane, pigeon or turkey.

input.text: The pupil in your eye is a narrow upright slit. If you are an American alligator, this is recorded for your species, and for the saltwater crocodile, whose slit pupil is described as mobile. If you are a Chinese alligator, you very likely have the same shape as your relative the American alligator, and for most other crocodiles and caimans nobody has recorded it.
input.note: Mobility of the pupil is stated only for the saltwater crocodile (R3), so I did not carry it to alligators.

input.text: A lamp that flashes 60 times a second looks steady to a human, and nobody has measured where flicker starts to look steady to you if you are a gray squirrel or a fox squirrel. The squirrels that have been measured differ a lot: a golden-mantled ground squirrel sees flicker above 100 flashes a second, an American red squirrel about 60, and a southern flying squirrel only 10 to 15.
input.note: Left out the chipmunk and California ground squirrel figures to keep the row short; the two golden-mantled records (120 and 108) are given as "above 100".

input.text: Nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before you stop seeing it as a flicker. Among the birds that share this view, it has been measured only in the rock pigeon, which sees flicker up to about 75 flashes a second, and in the domestic chicken, up to about 85, where a human stops at about 60. Those figures belong to those two birds and say nothing yet about you.
input.note: Grade i for herons, cranes and most others: no flicker record exists for them, and flicker speed only carries within a genus.

input.text: If you are a grey heron, a little egret, an intermediate egret, a Pacific reef egret or a Tick Bird, your head most often bobs once with each step you take. If you are a coot or a moorhen, it bobs when you swim as well as when you walk. For most other wading birds, nobody has recorded how your head moves.
input.note: Left out field-of-view figures: most species have none measured, and numbers do not carry between species.

input.text: If you are a peregrine falcon, you can see a light flicker even when it flashes at least 125 times a second, and a saker falcon sees it at about 100, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60. If you are a Harris's hawk, the figure is about 80. Nobody has measured how fast you see in any other hawk, eagle or falcon.
input.note: Left out a carried claim for other Falco species, since numbers may not travel between species.

input.text: If you are a cane toad, you strike at a small moving model of an insect, and if you are a bullfrog, you start to avoid an object coming at you when it spans about 20 degrees of your view. If you are a European toad, the cells that pick out moving prey respond less when a black and white textured background moves along with the prey at the same speed. Nobody has measured how movement looks to most other frogs and toads.
input.note: Left out R5 (quote does not state the result) and R3 (Japanese toad is not among the listed species).

input.text: If you are a red-tailed hawk, you read about 17 cycles a degree, a little over half of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Only a few other hawks, eagles, falcons and vultures have been measured, and their figures differ widely from species to species. If yours is not one of them, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out the 160 cycles a degree (R13) and the eagle and Egyptian vulture figures (R2, R4) because they belong to other species or have no named hawk. Nothing on interreceptor angle was recorded.

input.text: In the herons, egrets, moorhens and pigeons that have been measured, the part where both eyes see the same thing is a narrow upright strip in front of the bill, between about 20 and 35 degrees wide. If you are a black-crowned night heron, your two eyes together take in about 320 degrees around your head, and if you are a moorhen, about 300 degrees with a blind area behind your head. For most other waders, including the great blue heron, nobody has measured how wide your field of view is.
input.note: Left out the family-wide heron field width (R23, R24) and crane figure (R7) because field widths travel only within a genus.

input.text: If you are a cane toad, a light that flashes faster than about 7 times a second looks steady to you, where a human needs about 60 flashes a second before it looks steady. Other Rhinella toads, the cane toad's relatives in the same genus, very likely have a similarly low limit. Nobody has measured it in most other frogs and toads.
input.note: Only R1 (cane toad, 6.7 Hz) exists; the number is kept to the cane toad and the Rhinella sentence carries only the general ability.

input.text: If you are a white-tailed deer, you see four to six cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30, so fine detail is much blurrier for you. A reflective layer called the tapetum covers the upper part of your eye and overlaps the horizontal streak where you see most sharply. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see by, or how well you judge depth.
input.note: Acuity and tapetum are measured only in white-tailed deer here; dim-light sensitivity and depth have no deer record, so the row says so.

input.text: Your eyes sit on the sides of your head, so each one looks out in a different direction. Nobody has measured how wide an area you see at once, or how much the views of your two eyes overlap in front of you. Both have been measured in cattle, goats, giraffes and horses, but in no deer.
input.note: Left out the 310 degree figure (R10): it is an unsourced book line about deer in general, and field widths may only carry within a genus.

input.text: If you are an eastern gray squirrel, you can resolve stripes up to about 4 cycles a degree, and if you are a fox squirrel, about 2, where a human reads about 30. In the Eurasian red squirrel the cone cells are packed most densely in a horizontal streak with no sharp spot, and you very likely have the same if you belong to its genus, Sciurus, like the gray and fox squirrels. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is or how much of it both eyes share.
input.note: Left out the chipmunk and ground squirrel streak/best-vision figures since they cover other genera; the 3.9 figure comes from one gray squirrel.

input.text: Nobody has measured whether you have a sharp spot in your eye, or how sharply you see. In the saltwater crocodile, a relative in another genus, the sharpest vision lies along a streak that runs across the eye from the nose side to the rear side. That crocodile sees at best about 9 cycles a degree, about a third of the 30 a human sees.
input.note: Both figures are from saltwater crocodile only; the 9 is not carried to alligators because acuity travels only within a genus.

input.text: You very likely have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where humans have three. The Eurasian red squirrel, the California ground squirrel and the thirteen-lined ground squirrel all have two kinds, and in each of them the large majority of cones are one kind, with only a few of the other. If you are an eastern gray squirrel or a fox squirrel, your two kinds sense best in blue and in green.
input.note: Left out nanometer figures and any claim about which colors look alike, since no record states what dichromacy looks like for squirrels.

input.text: Your pupil, the opening that lets light into your eye, is a horizontal slit if you are a white-tailed deer, a red deer, a moose or a caribou. If you are a caribou, the slit opens into a round shape with about thirteen times the area when your pupil is fully open. Nobody has recorded the pupil of mule deer, roe deer or fallow deer.
input.note: Pupil shape is unrecorded for mule, roe and fallow deer, so the row says so; the area figure is caribou only.

input.text: What is known about reptile eyes comes from a few species, and they differ a lot. If you are a pond slider, you have four kinds of color-sensing cell, one of them for ultraviolet, and you see about 6 cycles a degree, where a human sees about 30. Nobody has measured how wide an area you see at once.
input.note: Left out pupil and fovea: they differ by species (circular pupils in four snakes and a turtle, a vertical one in the cottonmouth), so no single claim fits the whole view.

input.text: Nobody has measured how wide your view is, how sharply you see, how faint a light you can detect, or how you judge depth. A reflecting layer at the back of the eye, called a tapetum, has been found in the common caiman and the saltwater crocodile, and the caiman's retina looks adapted to dim light. In the saltwater crocodile the sharpest vision measured is about 9 cycles a degree, against about 30 for a human, and that figure belongs to that species alone.
input.note: Left out R4 (six crocodilian species, severely defocused underwater) because it does not name the alligator and optics only carry within a genus.

input.text: If you are a rock pigeon, you read about 12 cycles a degree, and if you are a mourning dove, about 7, where a human reads about 30. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are any other kind of bird, a heron, egret or crane included.
input.note: No record gives interreceptor angle for any species, so it is left out. Records for grouse, partridge and peafowl were not used because they are not relatives under the carry rules.

input.text: If you are a bullfrog, green frog, northern leopard frog, European common frog or European toad, your pupil is a horizontal almond-shaped slit, though a red-eyed treefrog has an upright one. If you are a northern leopard frog, you see about 3 cycles a degree, about a tenth of the 30 a human reads on an eye chart, and nobody has measured this in most other frogs and toads. Nobody has measured how wide your field of view is.
input.note: No record gives a field of view for any frog or toad, so the row says so.

input.text: If you are an American alligator, your cones hold four kinds of visual pigment, where a human has three. One of them senses green light best. The saltwater crocodile, a relative that has been measured, has three kinds of single cone, sensitive to violet, green and red.
input.note: Left out the 535 nm figure because it has no comparison job; the human count of three is general knowledge, not from a record.

input.text: Cattle, goats, sheep and horses have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three, and you very likely have two as well. In the white-tailed deer, one kind senses blue light best, and in the fallow deer the other kind senses green light best.
input.note: R6 (white-tailed deer) says cones and rods but gives no cone count, so I did not say deer were measured to have two kinds. Peak wavelengths left out as numbers.
